papers.title_in_file: QUANTUM-INSPIRED TENSOR NETWORK FOR EARTH SCIENCE
papers.what_it_is: A short conference paper that compresses a physics-informed neural network with a tensor-train decomposition and decomposes two hyperspectral satellite images with a CP decomposition.

assertions.value: The authors report that tensor-train compression reduced a physics-informed neural network for Burger's equation from 71, 101 parameters to 32, 701 parameters, and that the compressed network generated a solution with high accuracy such as the original network produced.
quotes: We reduced these 71, 101 parameters to 32, 701 parameters by compressing the odd numbers of the hidden layers by utilizing the TT-decomposition
the compressed PINN generated a solution to the Burger's equation with high accuracy such as having been produced by its original PINN
assertions.certainty_reason: One experiment on one benchmark PDE; accuracy is shown in Fig. 3 only, with no number in the text.
assertions.reader_inference: The method is quantum-inspired and classical; no quantum hardware or quantum model is run. The accuracy claim is qualitative.

assertions.value: The authors report that a CP decomposition gave a decomposition time of 0.1711 seconds, a compression ratio of 60 and an R-squared value of 0.9959 for the Indian Pine image, and 1.1013 seconds, a compression ratio of 140 and an R-squared value of 0.9450 for the Pavia University image.
quotes: For the Indian Pine HSI, the decomposition time was 0.1711 seconds, the compression ratio was 60, and the R-squared value between the raw and the decomposed Indian Pine HSI was 0.9959.
For the Pavia University HSI, the decomposition time was 1.1013 seconds, the compression ratio was 140, and the R-squared value between the raw and the decomposed Pavia University HSI was 0.9450.
assertions.certainty_reason: Single run per image on two datasets; no comparison with other compression methods.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper says the decomposition 'improved the spectral resolution'; the text reports only R-squared and compression, not a spectral-resolution metric.

assertions.value: The authors state that they used one benchmark PDE, Burger's equation, and two hyperspectral image datasets, Indian Pine and Pavia University.
quotes: As a benchmark PDE, we solved Burger's equation.
As practical satellite data, we employed HSIs of Indian Pine, USA and of Pavia University, Italy.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its scope (Abstract).
assertions.reader_inference: Results rest on one PDE and two images; no generalization claim is tested.

papers.title_in_file: Mapping quantum algorithms to multi-core quantum computing architectures
papers.what_it_is: A short paper that discusses circuit mapping for multi-core quantum computers and tests a graph-partitioning mapper over different core and qubit counts.

assertions.value: The authors report that more cores gave longer execution time and more non-local communications, and that the number of physical qubits is the most important factor for execution time, so a variable number of qubits per core is more efficient.
quotes: ii) The number of physical qubits is the most important factor regarding execution time and therefore, using a variable number of qubits per core is more efficient.
iii) The higher the number of cores, the longer the execution time and the higher the non-local communications.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result of one mapper on two benchmark circuits (Section IV, Fig. 3).

assertions.value: The authors state that they analyze the earlier mapping approach on different multi-core architectures with all-to-all qubit and core connectivity, using the Cuccaro adder and the QFT adder because their circuit characteristics are very dissimilar.
quotes: by considering different multi-core architecture designs with still all-to-all qubit and cores connectivity
In this paper, results for the Cuccaro and the QFT adder are presented as they have very dissimilar circuit characteristics.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own setup (Section IV).
assertions.reader_inference: Results hold only under all-to-all connectivity and two benchmark algorithms; routing inside cores is not tested.

assertions.value: The authors state that mapping performance depends highly on the quantum algorithm being executed.
quotes: Note also, that the performance highly depends on the quantum algorithm to be executed.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of a limit on its findings (Section V).

papers.title_in_file: MolQAE: Quantum Autoencoder for Molecular Representation Learning
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, experimental setup, results discussion (scaling analysis) and Conclusion; method section skimmed.
papers.what_it_is: A quantum autoencoder that maps SMILES strings to parameterized quantum states and is evaluated on QM9 for reconstruction fidelity.

assertions.value: The authors report that the 30-layer configuration with 4 latent qubits achieves 96.8% fidelity with 3,143 parameters.
assertions.anchor: Section IV, results discussion (Deep Quantum Architecture)
quotes: The extended evaluation at 20, 25, and 30 layers with 4 latent qubits reveals the true potential of deep quantum molecular autoencoders.
The 30-layer configuration achieves 96.8% fidelity with only 3,143 parameters
assertions.certainty_reason: Single-study empirical result.
assertions.reader_inference: Fidelity is reconstruction fidelity inside the model; no downstream task or classical autoencoder baseline appeared in the sections read.

assertions.value: The authors state that experiments used the QM9 dataset of approximately 134,000 organic molecules with up to 9 heavy atoms, an 8-qubit encoder with latent qubits from 1 to 7, and an implementation based on the TorchQuantum library.
quotes: Our molecular quantum autoencoder experiments were conducted using the QM9 molecular dataset [22], [23], containing approximately 134,000 organic molecules with up to 9 heavy atoms.
The quantum autoencoder architecture employed 8 encoder qubits with varying latent qubits (1-7)
Our implementation is based on TorchQuantum library [24]
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own setup (Section IV).
assertions.reader_inference: TorchQuantum is a simulator library; no hardware run was seen in the sections read.

assertions.value: The authors report that fidelity saturates at 96.8% and that further circuit depth gave only 0.9% marginal improvement, which they take to mean added depth cannot overcome fundamental encoding constraints.
quotes: information capacity limit, with only 0.9% marginal improvement, indicating that additional circuit depth cannot overcome fundamental encoding constraints.
The saturation at 96.8% fidelity represents a fundamental breakthrough in understanding quantum molecular representation limits.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical saturation from one fit; the 'fundamental' interpretation is the authors' own.
assertions.reader_inference: The 'theoretical ceiling' wording is not backed by a derivation in the sections read.

assertions.value: The authors claim that their results establish quantum advantage in parameter efficiency for molecular representation learning.
quotes: This demonstrates that quantum circuits leverage superposition and entanglement mechanisms rather than brute-force parameter scaling, establishing quantum advantage in parameter efficiency for molecular representation learning.
assertions.certainty_reason: Author claim; no classical baseline comparison was found in the sections read.
assertions.reader_inference: A scaling fit on a simulated model does not by itself show advantage over classical autoencoders.

papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, experimental setting, experiment results (success probability), Conclusion; derivations skimmed.
papers.what_it_is: A quantum multi-programming version of Grover's search that runs partial-diffusion circuits in parallel, tested on IBM superconducting machines.

assertions.value: The paper proves that the new algorithm increases the rotation angle of the Grover operator, which increases the success probability.
quotes: We proved that this new algorithm increases the rotation angle of the Grover operator which, as a result, increases the success probability.
This new algorithm has a bigger rotation angle than the angle of the canonical Grover operator as shown in Eq. (12).
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated as proved in the Abstract; Eq. (12) in Section 3 (derivation not checked by the reader).

assertions.value: The authors report that on IBM Washington the QMP circuits' measured success probability rose from 12.0% (default mapping) and 20.1% (manual mapping) for G2D3M3 to 41.6% (default) and 70.1% (manual) for G3D2M2, while the canonical Grover circuits D5M5 and D5D5M5 measured 2.3% and 3.1%.
quotes: The theoretical success probabilities of D5M5 and D5D5M5 are 25.8% and 60.2%, respectively (Eq. (5)). On the other hand, because of the quantum noise, their measured success probabilities (2.3% and 3.1%, respectively as shown in Fig. 6)
the QMP circuits show a big increase in success probabilities from G2D3M3 (12.0% for QMP (default) and 20.1% for QMP (manual)) to G3D2M2 (41.6% for QMP (default) and 70.1% for QMP (manual)).
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical hardware result for a single five-qubit search problem (one target of 32), averaged over 30 repetitions.
assertions.reader_inference: The comparison uses 24 to 48 qubits against 6, and the paper's own metric (EQCV) is introduced to account for this; the result is for one problem size.

assertions.value: The authors state that experiments ran on IBM Washington (127 qubits, 64 QV) and IBMQ Brooklyn (65 qubits and 32 QV), with 8192 trials (shots) and 30 running repetitions.
quotes: We conducted the experiments of the designed quantum circuits on the two IBM quantum computers including IBM Washington (127 qubits, 64 QV) and IBMQ Brooklyn (65 qubits and 32 QV).
The experiments were performed with 8192 trials (shots) and 30 running repetitions
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own setup (Section 4.3).

assertions.value: The authors state that the number of blocks in the QMP is limited by the qubit count of the target processor and the search problem size, and that applying QMP to a quantum algorithm is not straightforward because it needs a decomposition of the algorithm.
quotes: The number of blocks in the QMP is limited by the number of qubits of the target quantum processor and the search problem size
applying QMP to a quantum algorithm is not straightforward because it needs a decomposition of the algorithm.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of limits (Section 5).

papers.title_in_file: Quantum Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Autonomous Mobility Cooperation
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, limitations section, simulation results and scalability section, Conclusion; application scenario text skimmed.
papers.what_it_is: A magazine-style paper proposing a quantum actor-critic multi-agent reinforcement learning scheme with a projection value measure, evaluated in simulation.

assertions.value: The authors report that over 1,000 epochs the proposed QMARL achieved the highest reward and fastest convergence against four benchmarks, including a classical MARL with 110 parameters and a classical MARL with 40,000 parameters.
assertions.anchor: Section on performance evaluation, Fig. 3 and Table I
quotes: Fig. 3 shows the dynamics in total rewards over 1,000 epochs. Based on this result, it can be confirmed that the proposed framework achieves the highest reward and the fastest convergence compared to other benchmark frameworks.
Comp2 refers to the classical MARL framework utilizing 110 parameters where the number is equivalent to the one of our proposed framework and Comp1.
Comp3 is also a classical MARL framework whereas it has much larger parameters, i.e., 40,000
assertions.certainty_reason: Single simulation study; the figure holds the numbers, and the text gives no variance.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper calls this result 'quantum supremacy'; a parameter-count comparison in simulation is not a computational-advantage proof.

assertions.value: The authors report that conventional MARL outperformed its counterparts when the number of actions was relatively small, and that QMARL with the projection value measure prevailed at a higher action dimension.
assertions.anchor: Section on logarithmic-scale dimension reduction, Table II
quotes: the conventional MARL-based approach outperforms its counterparts across all benchmarks when the number of actions is relatively small (21 and 24).
When the action space is with a higher dimension (216) which can well-suited for real-world scenarios, the proposed QMARL-based approach utilizing PVM prevails in comparison.
assertions.certainty_reason: Single simulation study (Table II); the action counts are exponents, shown in the PDF as superscripts.
assertions.reader_inference: The quantum scheme won only at the largest action space tested; at the smaller ones the classical method was better.

assertions.value: The authors state that the number of input qubits usable in a QMARL model is extremely restricted, which leads to poor performance, and that the error and scale issues cannot be resolved in modern QC and QMARL.
assertions.anchor: Section II-A.2 (Limitations to QC/QMARL in the NISQ Era)
quotes: the number of input qubits that can be used in a QMARL model is extremely restricted, which leads to poor performance.
These error and scale related issues cannot be resolved in modern QC and QMARL
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of a limit on its approach (Section II-A.2).

papers.title_in_file: Quantum Neural Networks for Cloud Cover Parameterizations in Climate Models
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, results summary on performance, and the Conclusion/outlook; appendices and method details skimmed.
papers.what_it_is: A comparison of quantum neural networks and classical neural networks as cloud cover parameterizations trained on ICON climate-model data.

assertions.value: The authors report that the overall performance of the investigated QNNs is comparable to that of classical NNs with the same number of trainable parameters, with both outperforming standard parameterizations used in climate models.
quotes: Our results show that the overall performance of the investigated QNNs is comparable to that of classical NNs of similar size, i.e., with the same number of trainable parameters, with both ansatzes outperforming standard parameterizations used in climate models.
assertions.certainty_reason: Single-study empirical result on one dataset.
assertions.reader_inference: The result is parity with classical networks, not an advantage.

assertions.value: The authors report that their QNNs train stably in the presence of shot noise.
quotes: We show that our QNNs can train stably even in presence of shot noise
assertions.certainty_reason: Single-study empirical result.
assertions.reader_inference: Shot noise is sampling noise only; hardware gate noise is not covered by this statement.

assertions.value: The authors state that their architecture search is not exhaustive, that their QNNs show similar performance to classical networks at least in the noiseless setting, and that it is largely unknown which classical datasets suit quantum learning models better than classical ones.
quotes: we are aware that our architecture search is not exhaustive
Overall, the investigated QNNs show a similar performance (at least in the noiseless setting) to classical NNs in all these aspects
it is to a large extent unknown what types of classical datasets are better suited to quantum learning models than to a classical ones
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of scope and limits in the outlook section.

papers.title_in_file: Limitations of Quantum Advantage in Unsupervised Machine Learning
papers.version_note: The file is arXiv:2511.10709v2 dated 13 May 2026; its folder and name say 2025.
papers.what_it_is: A short theoretical analysis of when replacing classical probability distributions with quantum density matrices can give a quantum advantage in Boltzmann-machine style unsupervised learning.

assertions.value: The paper states that an advantage can be obtained only when features of density matrices that are absent in classical probability distributions are exploited, and that such situations depend on the input data and the targeted observables.
quotes: An advantage can be obtained only when features of density matrices that are absent in classical probability distributions are exploited.
Such situations depend on the input data as well as the targeted observables.
assertions.certainty_reason: Analytic argument in Sections III and IV (commuting case reduces to the classical analysis).

assertions.value: The paper states that the hidden degrees of freedom can provide only classical advantage when the visible state maximises quantum advantage.
quotes: The hidden degrees of freedom can then provide only classical advantage.
assertions.certainty_reason: Follows from the Schmidt decomposition argument in Section IV.
assertions.reader_inference: Adding hidden units to a Boltzmann machine is then not a source of quantum advantage under this analysis.

assertions.value: The paper states that its constraints on unsupervised learning can be relaxed when the input data are quantum in nature.
quotes: The constraints on unsupervised learning obtained here can be relaxed, when the input data are quantum in nature (the output is always classical).
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of the scope of its result (Section IV).
assertions.reader_inference: The limits apply to classical input data.

papers.version_note: The file is arXiv:2302.00566v3 dated 8 Aug 2024; its folder and name say 2023.
papers.partial_detail: Abstract/introduction, results summary for the datasets, and Conclusion; circuit and algorithm sections skimmed.
papers.what_it_is: Two quantum clustering algorithms, a divisive hierarchical one and an unsharp-measurement one, tested in simulation on three datasets.

assertions.value: The authors report that UMCA reached an accuracy of approximately 94% on the labeled Wisconsin breast cancer dataset of 699 datapoints, using only 4 qubits and measurements polynomial in qubit numbers.
quotes: UMCA is implemented on the labeled Wisconsin breast cancer dataset of 699 datapoints, and where we found an accuracy of approximately 94%, using only 4 qubits and measurements polynomial in qubit numbers.
assertions.certainty_reason: Single-study simulated result on one dataset.
assertions.reader_inference: No classical clustering baseline accuracy on this dataset appears in the sections read.

assertions.value: The authors report that QHCA gave better results than classical divisive clustering on a linearly non-separable dataset, even with a very low number of measurements, and clustered the Churritz cities dataset with only 7 qubits.
quotes: We have shown that QHCA provides better results than the classical divisive clustering on the linearly non-separable dataset, even with very low number of measurements.
We further showed that for the Churritz cities dataset, the algorithm is able to cluster with only 7 qubits.
assertions.certainty_reason: Single-study simulated results on small datasets.
assertions.reader_inference: The comparison is against classical divisive clustering only, not against k-means or DBSCAN.

assertions.value: The authors state that they used a statevector simulator and a QASM simulator, and that realization of the algorithms on a real quantum device is beyond the scope of the paper.
quotes: We have used both statevector simulator and the QASM simulator for the implementation of QHCA on the concentric circle dataset.
the realization of the algorithms on a real quantum device is beyond the scope of this paper
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of scope (Section 5).
assertions.reader_inference: The NISQ-friendly label rests on simulation and an assumed measurement error, not on hardware runs.
